# Literature Review

Does critique severity change revision success under fixed inference budgets and constant politeness? Scope: empirical LLM critique, error detection, tone and relevant measurement work, primarily 2023–2026. Exclude opinion pieces and unrelated training-only methods.

## Key papers

- **Madaan et al. (NeurIPS 2023), Self-Refine.** A single model drafts, gives actionable feedback and revises. Seven tasks include dialogue, constrained generation, code, sentiment reversal and math. Human preferences and task-specific scores give an average reported gain of about 20 percentage points over one-step generation. The one-step baseline leaves a compute difference and the aggregate combines dissimilar outcomes. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651) · [Code](https://github.com/madaan/self-refine)
- **Huang et al. (ICLR 2024), Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet.** Compare intrinsic revision and oracle-triggered revision for GSM8K, CommonSenseQA and HotpotQA, using answer accuracy and transition counts. Correct drafts can degrade, and extra attempts with self-consistency compete with debate. On GSM8K, GPT-3.5 moves from 75.9% to 74.7% after two intrinsic rounds. Prompt design and old model snapshots limit transfer. [Paper](https://openreview.net/forum?id=IkmD3fKBPQ)
- **Tyen et al. (Findings ACL 2024), LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location.** Annotate first errors across five BIG-Bench reasoning tasks, then compare prompting for fault localization with backtracking using known error locations. Ground-truth locations improve downstream task accuracy across the five tasks. Correct-trace and incorrect-trace detection performance differ, so score false alarms and misses separately. The traces come from an upstream model and localization assumes a step segmentation. [Paper](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.826/) · [Code and data](https://github.com/WHGTyen/BIG-Bench-Mistake)
- **Lin et al. (Findings ACL 2024), CriticBench.** Across 15 datasets in five domains, score generation, critique and correction for 17 models on responses from three model families. The baselines include direct generation and zero-/few-shot critique and correction. Critique and correction vary by task and model. The appendix documents response filtering, rule-versus-judge disagreements and task-specific prompts. Mixed evaluators complicate cross-domain comparisons. [Paper](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.91/) · [Project and code](https://criticbench.github.io/)
- **Yin et al. (2024), Should We Respect LLMs?** Eight human-ranked levels of politeness in English, Chinese and Japanese, evaluated using summarization, multiple-choice understanding (MMLU, C-Eval and JMMLU) and stereotype-bias tasks. Impoliteness often degrades results, and the best level varies by language and task. Examples also vary directive wording, which motivates checking severity and politeness independently. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14531)
- **Gou et al. (ICLR 2024), CRITIC.** Compare tool-assisted revision with direct generation and tool-free revision for open-domain QA, math program synthesis and detoxification. External search, execution and feedback signals improve task outcomes, as measured with answer, execution or toxicity metrics. Tool access changes evidence and inference cost together, making this a grounding reference for the current study. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738) · [Code](https://github.com/microsoft/ProphetNet/tree/master/CRITIC)
- **Zhang and Li (2026 preprint), Should I Be Polite to My LLM Relevance Judge?** Evaluate 3,498 TREC DL19/DL20 pairs across eight relevance judges, five calibrated tone levels and three paraphrases per level. Weighted agreement can move with judge leniency while average ranking shifts are small. Most models show small effects, and one shows a U-shaped pattern. This motivates testing critic false-positive rates, although the study ends at relevance judgments. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09703)

## Methods, baselines and evidence gaps

Self-Refine provides actionable, generic and absent-feedback variants. Huang et al. show why a draft-only score and compute-matched alternatives are both useful. Their Appendix A illustrates real repairs, fabricated objections and unchanged answers. Their CommonGen-Hard examples also show that an unusually restricted initial prompt can inflate measured improvement. CriticBench's prompts in Appendix G and its data-quality checks in Appendices B–F show why identical output schemas and robust extraction matter. Tyen et al. separate detection accuracy, false-positive behavior and revision success. Their backtracking uses up to eight regenerations, so its raw gains cannot be attributed to a one-revision severity intervention. Yin et al.'s Appendix B questionnaire and Appendix C prompt rankings offer a starting point for blinded tone checks. Zhang and Li use cross-fitting to check whether shifts in leniency track agreement on held-out judgments. In the screened studies, the combination of fixed per-call caps, shared drafts and tone-calibrated severity remains untested.

## Experiment recommendations

1. **Estimate the severity curve.** Pair low, medium and high scrutiny on each frozen draft for GSM8K and IFEval. Keep the same sentence structure, register, number of finding slots, draft/critique/revision cap, model snapshot and generation settings. Vary audit thresholds from clear material defects, through consequential underjustification, to vulnerable assumptions or omitted checks. Allow abstention and prohibit unsupported claims in every arm. Use multiple matched templates and randomly order arms. Blinded ratings should confirm a severity gradient and tone equivalence within a predeclared margin on generated critiques as well as prompts.
2. **Measure when scrutiny helps.** On BIG-Bench Mistake, score exact first-error index, error-present recall and false alarms on clean traces. Cross-tabulate clean/flawed traces against upstream and revised final-answer accuracy. Where feasible, compare to a separately identified oracle-location diagnostic with the same revision cap. Use the oracle only as a reference for diagnostic quality.
3. **Hold the evidence fixed.** Generate one candidate finding independent of treatment and reuse its text, span and graded evidence across randomized policy variants. Change the threshold for recommending revision with a fixed schema and politeness. Compare edit uptake and correctness, including on model-generated false alarms. Treat this as an intervention on disposition conditional on the stored candidate, since discovery was held fixed by design.

Use draft-only as a descriptive reference. Add one-shot at the total output allowance and critique-free revision with the freed critic allowance available to the solver as budgeted controls. Report per-stage input, visible output and any billed reasoning tokens, plus stop reasons and truncation. Equal output caps define the primary intention-to-treat budget. Actual consumption can vary with early EOS, so report it by arm and check conclusions in a prespecified length-balanced sensitivity analysis. Do not infer compute equality from output caps alone.

Primary metrics are GSM8K numeric accuracy and IFEval strict prompt accuracy. Also report strict instruction accuracy, repair among incorrect drafts, damage among correct drafts, and paired risk differences with item-level bootstrap intervals. Stratify by task and test severity-by-task interaction using paired contrasts. Compare adjacent levels and a curvature contrast instead of assuming monotonicity. Treat edit distance, changed answers or constraint satisfaction, repetition, self-reference, hedging and question counts as observable behavior. Normalize counts by text length. Audit a blinded subset for substantive fixes versus surface edits. Similar but held-out problem variants can probe transfer if included in the fixed evaluation design. Text markers alone cannot establish internal effort or understanding.

## Search and screening

Search date 2026-11-24. Keywords included self-refinement, intrinsic self-correction, critique-correct reasoning, mistake localization, feedback quality, prompt politeness, severity operating point, compute-matched revision, and instruction-following evaluation. Paper-finder returned a service-unavailable error. Manual web discovery used arXiv and ACL/ICLR proceedings, with Semantic Scholar and Google Scholar discovery queries, plus implementation and benchmark searches using Papers with Code terms. Primary PDFs supported the retained claims. The seven retained papers cover five direct design references and two baseline references. The similarly titled CriticBench preprint arXiv:2402.13764 assesses a different critique benchmark and was screened out in favor of the critique-correct reasoning paper. A survey helped orient discovery, while the review cites the original studies for experimental findings. Media reports were excluded.

# Hypothesis Generation

Structured frameworks for developing research hypotheses and experimental designs.

## When to Use

- Starting a new research project
- Developing research questions
- Planning experiments
- Generating testable predictions
- Exploring competing explanations

## Hypothesis Framework

### Good Hypothesis Characteristics

A strong research hypothesis should be:

1. **Specific**: Clear, precise statement
2. **Testable**: Can be validated with data
3. **Falsifiable**: Can potentially be proven wrong
4. **Grounded**: Based on prior knowledge/theory
5. **Novel**: Adds something new to the field

### Hypothesis Types

| Type | Description | Example |
|------|-------------|---------|
| **Descriptive** | Describes a phenomenon | "LLMs exhibit X behavior on task Y" |
| **Relational** | Proposes relationship | "Factor A correlates with outcome B" |
| **Causal** | Claims causation | "Intervention X causes improvement Y" |
| **Comparative** | Compares conditions | "Method A outperforms method B on task C" |
| **Mechanistic** | Explains how/why | "Effect X occurs because of mechanism Y" |

## Hypothesis Development Process

### Step 1: Identify the Gap

From your literature review, identify:
- What is known
- What is unknown or unclear
- What is contradictory

Document the gap:
```markdown
## Research Gap
**Known**: [What prior work has established]
**Unknown**: [What remains to be discovered]
**Our Focus**: [Which unknown we address]
```

### Step 2: Generate Initial Hypotheses

Use these prompts:
- "If [assumption] is true, then we should observe [prediction]"
- "Based on [theory/observation], we expect [outcome]"
- "Contrary to [current belief], we propose [alternative]"

Generate multiple hypotheses (aim for 3-5 initially).

### Step 3: Develop Competing Hypotheses

For each hypothesis, identify:
- **Alternative explanations**: What else could explain the same observation?
- **Null hypothesis**: What if there's no effect?
- **Opposite hypothesis**: What if the effect is reversed?

### Step 4: Operationalize

Convert abstract hypothesis to concrete, measurable terms:

| Abstract | Operationalized |
|----------|-----------------|
| "LLMs understand X" | "GPT-4 achieves >80% accuracy on benchmark Y" |
| "Method A is better" | "Method A improves F1 by >5% over baseline B" |
| "Training affects X" | "Models trained with X show Y behavior increase" |

### Step 5: Design Tests

For each hypothesis, define:
- **Data**: What data is needed?
- **Method**: How will you test?
- **Metrics**: What measures success/failure?
- **Threshold**: What counts as support/rejection?

## Competing Hypotheses Framework

### Template

```markdown
## Research Question
[Your main question]

### Hypothesis 1: [Name]
**Statement**: [Formal hypothesis]
**Rationale**: [Why this might be true]
**Prediction**: [What we expect to observe]
**Test**: [How to test]

### Hypothesis 2: [Alternative]
**Statement**: [Formal hypothesis]
**Rationale**: [Why this might be true]
**Prediction**: [What we expect to observe]
**Test**: [How to test]

### Hypothesis 3: [Null]
**Statement**: There is no significant effect
**Prediction**: No difference between conditions
**Test**: Statistical significance testing

### Decision Matrix
| Outcome | Supports H1 | Supports H2 | Supports H3 |
|---------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| [Result A] | Yes | No | No |
| [Result B] | No | Yes | No |
| [Result C] | No | No | Yes |
```

## Experimental Design

### Variables

| Type | Definition | Example |
|------|------------|---------|
| **Independent (IV)** | What you manipulate | Model type, training data |
| **Dependent (DV)** | What you measure | Accuracy, F1, latency |
| **Controlled** | Held constant | Prompt template, temperature |
| **Confounding** | Could affect DV | Data contamination, model size |

### Design Types

**Between-subjects**: Different conditions get different treatments
- Pros: No carryover effects
- Cons: Need more samples, individual differences

**Within-subjects**: Same subject gets all treatments
- Pros: Controls individual differences
- Cons: Order effects, fatigue

**Factorial**: Multiple IVs crossed
- Pros: Tests interactions
- Cons: More conditions needed

### Control Strategies

1. **Baseline comparison**: Compare against known baseline
2. **Ablation study**: Remove components to test necessity
3. **Randomization**: Random assignment to conditions
4. **Counterbalancing**: Vary order across subjects/trials

## Prediction Documentation

### Template for Each Hypothesis

```markdown
## Hypothesis: [Name]

### Formal Statement
[If X, then Y under conditions Z]

### Background
[Why we think this might be true]

### Predictions

#### Primary Prediction
- **Measure**: [What to measure]
- **Expected outcome**: [Specific prediction]
- **Threshold for support**: [Quantitative criterion]

#### Secondary Predictions
1. [Additional prediction 1]
2. [Additional prediction 2]

### Potential Confounds
- [Confound 1]: [How to address]
- [Confound 2]: [How to address]

### What Would Falsify This?
[Specific outcomes that would reject hypothesis]
```

## Common Pitfalls

### Avoid These

1. **Vague hypotheses**: "Method A is good" → "Method A achieves >X on benchmark Y"
2. **Unfalsifiable claims**: "LLMs may sometimes..." → "LLMs will show X in condition Y"
3. **Post-hoc hypothesizing**: Generating hypothesis after seeing data
4. **Confirmation bias**: Only looking for supporting evidence
5. **Missing null hypothesis**: Not considering "no effect" possibility

### Warning Signs

- Hypothesis can explain any outcome
- No clear way to measure
- Based on single observation
- Ignores contradictory evidence
- No alternative hypotheses considered

## Quality Checklist

- [ ] Hypothesis is specific and clear
- [ ] Hypothesis is testable with available resources
- [ ] Hypothesis is falsifiable
- [ ] Hypothesis is grounded in prior work
- [ ] Alternative hypotheses identified
- [ ] Null hypothesis specified
- [ ] Variables operationalized
- [ ] Confounds identified and addressed
- [ ] Success/failure criteria defined
- [ ] Predictions documented before experimentation

## References

See `references/` folder for:
- `hypothesis_templates.md`: Templates for different research types

# Data Analysis

Guidance for exploratory data analysis and statistical testing.

## When to Use

- Exploring new datasets
- Selecting appropriate statistical tests
- Performing power analysis
- Reporting results in papers
- Validating experimental results

## Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

### EDA Workflow

1. **Load and Inspect**: Basic data structure
2. **Summarize**: Descriptive statistics
3. **Visualize**: Distributions and relationships
4. **Identify Issues**: Missing data, outliers
5. **Document Findings**: Key insights

### Initial Inspection

```python
# Basic checks
df.shape          # Dimensions
df.dtypes         # Data types
df.head()         # First rows
df.describe()     # Summary stats
df.isnull().sum() # Missing values
```

### Key Questions to Answer

| Question | What to Check |
|----------|---------------|
| What's the size? | Rows, columns, data types |
| Any missing data? | Null counts, patterns |
| What's the distribution? | Histograms, descriptive stats |
| Any outliers? | Box plots, z-scores |
| Any relationships? | Correlations, scatter plots |
| Any patterns? | Trends, clusters, groups |

### Visualization Guide

| Data Type | Visualization |
|-----------|---------------|
| Single continuous | Histogram, density plot, box plot |
| Single categorical | Bar chart, pie chart |
| Two continuous | Scatter plot, line plot |
| Two categorical | Grouped bar chart, heatmap |
| Continuous + categorical | Box plot by group, violin plot |
| Time series | Line plot with time axis |

## Statistical Test Selection

### Decision Tree

```
Question: What are you trying to do?
│
├─ Compare groups
│   │
│   ├─ How many groups?
│   │   ├─ 2 groups → See "Two Group Comparisons"
│   │   └─ 3+ groups → See "Multiple Group Comparisons"
│   │
│   └─ Related or independent?
│       ├─ Independent (different subjects)
│       └─ Related (same subjects, before/after)
│
├─ Examine relationships
│   ├─ Two variables → Correlation, regression
│   └─ Multiple variables → Multiple regression
│
└─ Test proportions
    └─ Chi-square test
```

### Two Group Comparisons

| Data Type | Independent Groups | Related Groups |
|-----------|-------------------|----------------|
| **Normal** | Independent t-test | Paired t-test |
| **Non-normal** | Mann-Whitney U | Wilcoxon signed-rank |

### Multiple Group Comparisons

| Data Type | Independent Groups | Related Groups |
|-----------|-------------------|----------------|
| **Normal** | One-way ANOVA | Repeated measures ANOVA |
| **Non-normal** | Kruskal-Wallis | Friedman test |

### Checking Assumptions

**Normality Tests**:
- Shapiro-Wilk (n < 50)
- Kolmogorov-Smirnov (n ≥ 50)
- Visual: Q-Q plot

**Homogeneity of Variance**:
- Levene's test
- Visual: Box plots by group

**Independence**:
- By experimental design
- Durbin-Watson (for residuals)

### When Assumptions Fail

| Violation | Solution |
|-----------|----------|
| Non-normality | Non-parametric test, transformation |
| Unequal variance | Welch's t-test, transformation |
| Non-independence | Mixed-effects model |
| Outliers | Robust methods, removal (with justification) |

## Effect Sizes

### Why Effect Sizes Matter

- p-values tell you if effect exists, not how big
- Effect sizes quantify the magnitude
- Required for power analysis
- Better for meta-analysis

### Common Effect Sizes

| Measure | Context | Interpretation |
|---------|---------|----------------|
| **Cohen's d** | Two means | 0.2=small, 0.5=medium, 0.8=large |
| **Pearson's r** | Correlation | 0.1=small, 0.3=medium, 0.5=large |
| **Eta-squared** | ANOVA | 0.01=small, 0.06=medium, 0.14=large |
| **Odds ratio** | Categorical | 1.5=small, 2.5=medium, 4=large |

### Computing Effect Sizes

```python
# Cohen's d for two groups
import numpy as np

def cohens_d(group1, group2):
    n1, n2 = len(group1), len(group2)
    var1, var2 = np.var(group1, ddof=1), np.var(group2, ddof=1)
    pooled_std = np.sqrt(((n1-1)*var1 + (n2-1)*var2) / (n1+n2-2))
    return (np.mean(group1) - np.mean(group2)) / pooled_std
```

## Power Analysis

### Key Concepts

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| **Power** | Probability of detecting true effect (1-β) |
| **α (alpha)** | False positive rate (typically 0.05) |
| **β (beta)** | False negative rate (typically 0.20) |
| **Effect size** | Magnitude of effect |
| **Sample size** | Number of observations |

### Power Analysis Uses

1. **A priori**: Before study, determine needed sample size
2. **Post hoc**: After study, calculate achieved power
3. **Sensitivity**: Given n and power, what effect detectable?

### Sample Size Calculation

```python
from statsmodels.stats.power import TTestIndPower

analysis = TTestIndPower()

# Sample size for t-test
n = analysis.solve_power(
    effect_size=0.5,    # Cohen's d
    alpha=0.05,         # Significance level
    power=0.80,         # Desired power
    ratio=1.0,          # n2/n1
    alternative='two-sided'
)
```

### Power Guidelines

| Power | Interpretation |
|-------|----------------|
| < 0.50 | Inadequate |
| 0.50-0.70 | Low |
| 0.70-0.80 | Moderate |
| ≥ 0.80 | Adequate (standard target) |
| ≥ 0.90 | High |

## Multiple Comparisons

### The Problem

- Each test has α chance of false positive
- Multiple tests inflate false positive rate
- Family-wise error rate: 1-(1-α)^n

### Correction Methods

| Method | When to Use | Strictness |
|--------|-------------|------------|
| **Bonferroni** | Few comparisons | Most conservative |
| **Holm** | Few comparisons | Less conservative |
| **Benjamini-Hochberg** | Many comparisons | Controls FDR |
| **Tukey HSD** | Post-hoc ANOVA | Common choice |

### Applying Corrections

```python
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

# Bonferroni
adjusted_alpha = 0.05 / num_tests

# Holm-Bonferroni
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
reject, pvals_corrected, _, _ = multipletests(pvals, method='holm')

# Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR)
reject, pvals_corrected, _, _ = multipletests(pvals, method='fdr_bh')
```

## Reporting Results

### APA Format

**t-test**:
```
t(df) = X.XX, p = .XXX, d = X.XX
```
Example: t(45) = 2.34, p = .023, d = 0.68

**ANOVA**:
```
F(df1, df2) = X.XX, p = .XXX, η² = .XX
```
Example: F(2, 87) = 4.56, p = .013, η² = .095

**Correlation**:
```
r(df) = .XX, p = .XXX
```
Example: r(48) = .42, p = .003

**Chi-square**:
```
χ²(df, N = n) = X.XX, p = .XXX
```
Example: χ²(2, N = 150) = 6.78, p = .034

### Reporting Guidelines

**Do**:
- Report exact p-values (not just < .05)
- Include effect sizes
- Report confidence intervals
- Describe what was tested

**Don't**:
- Say "proved" or "significant difference" alone
- Report only significant results
- Cherry-pick tests
- Over-interpret p = .049 vs p = .051

### Results Table Format

```
Table 1: Comparison of Methods on Benchmark X

Method      Mean (SD)       95% CI          Effect Size
------------------------------------------------------
Baseline    75.2 (3.4)     [73.1, 77.3]    -
Method A    78.9 (2.8)*    [77.2, 80.6]    d = 0.52
Method B    81.4 (3.1)**   [79.5, 83.3]    d = 0.89

Note: * p < .05, ** p < .01 vs Baseline
```

## Common Pitfalls

| Pitfall | Problem | Solution |
|---------|---------|----------|
| P-hacking | Running tests until significant | Pre-register analysis |
| HARKing | Hypothesizing after results known | State hypotheses before |
| Multiple comparisons | Inflated false positives | Apply correction |
| Pseudo-replication | Non-independent samples | Mixed-effects models |
| Ignoring effect sizes | Significant ≠ important | Report effect sizes |

## Quality Checklist

- [ ] Research questions clearly stated
- [ ] Appropriate test selected and justified
- [ ] Assumptions checked
- [ ] Sample size justified (power analysis)
- [ ] Multiple comparisons corrected
- [ ] Effect sizes reported
- [ ] Confidence intervals included
- [ ] Results correctly interpreted
- [ ] Limitations acknowledged

## References

See `references/` folder for:
- `test_selection.md`: Detailed test selection guide
- `apa_reporting.md`: Complete APA reporting templates

BIG-Bench Mistake includes 478 null-index traces and 51 blank upstream answers (50 Dyck and one logical deduction). Preserve these in localization. def iterative_gsm(question: str, max_attempts: int, feedback_type: str, temperature: float):

    # initialize all the required components

    # generation of the first fast version
    task_init = GSMInit(engine=ENGINE, prompt_examples="data/prompt/gsm/init.txt", temperature=temperature)

    # getting feedback
    if feedback_type == "naive":
        raise NotImplementedError
    else:
        task_feedback = GSMFeedback(engine=ENGINE, prompt_examples="data/prompt/gsm/feedback.txt", temperature=0.7)


    n_attempts = 0

    log = []

    while n_attempts < max_attempts:

        if n_attempts == 0:
            solution = task_init(solution=question)

        fb_and_maybe_soln = task_feedback(solution=solution)
        

        log.append({"attempt": n_attempts, "solution_curr": solution, "solution_fixed": fb_and_maybe_soln["solution"], "feedback": fb_and_maybe_soln["feedback"]})

        if "it is correct" in fb_and_maybe_soln["feedback"].lower():
            break

        solution = fb_and_maybe_soln["solution"]

        n_attempts += 1

    return log


def fix_gsm(gsm_task_file: str, max_attempts: int, outfile: str, feedback_type: str, temperature: float):


    slow_programs_df = pd.read_json(gsm_task_file, lines=True, orient="records")
    slow_programs_df["run_logs"] = None
    results = []
    for i, row in tqdm(slow_programs_df.iterrows(), total=len(slow_programs_df)):
        row_copy = row.to_dict()
        try:
            run_logs = iterative_gsm(question=row["input"], max_attempts=max_attempts, feedback_type=feedback_type, temperature=temperature)

            row_copy["generated_answer_ours"] = run_logs[-1]["solution_fixed"]
            row_copy["generated_answer_direct"] = run_logs[0]["solution_curr"]
            results.append(row_copy)
            if i % 10 == 0:
                pd.DataFrame(results).to_json(outfile + f".{i}.jsonl", orient="records", lines=True)
        except Exception as e:
            # raise e
            pass

CODEX = "code-davinci-002"
# GPT3 = "text-davinci-003"
ENGINE = CODEX


@retry_parse_fail_prone_cmd
def iterative_gsm(question: str, max_attempts: int, feedback_type: str, temperature: float):

    # initialize all the required components

    # generation of the first fast version
    task_init = GSMInit(engine=ENGINE, prompt_examples="data/prompt/gsm/init.txt", temperature=temperature)

    # getting feedback
    if feedback_type == "naive":
        raise NotImplementedError
    else:
        task_feedback = GSMFeedback(engine=ENGINE, prompt_examples="data/prompt/gsm/feedback.txt", temperature=0.7)


    n_attempts = 0

    log = []

    while n_attempts < max_attempts:

        if n_attempts == 0:
            solution = task_init(solution=question)

        fb_and_maybe_soln = task_feedback(solution=solution)
        

        log.append({"attempt": n_attempts, "solution_curr": solution, "solution_fixed": fb_and_maybe_soln["solution"], "feedback": fb_and_maybe_soln["feedback"]})

        if "it is correct" in fb_and_maybe_soln["feedback"].lower():
            break

        solution = fb_and_maybe_soln["solution"]

        n_attempts += 1

    return log


def fix_gsm(gsm_task_file: str, max_attempts: int, outfile: str, feedback_type: str, temperature: float):


    slow_programs_df = pd.read_json(gsm_task_file, lines=True, orient="records")
    slow_programs_df["run_logs"] = None
    results = []
    for i, row in tqdm(slow_programs_df.iterrows(), total=len(slow_programs_df)):
        row_copy = row.to_dict()
        try:
            run_logs = iterative_gsm(question=row["input"], max_attempts=max_attempts, feedback_type=feedback_type, temperature=temperature)
            row_copy["run_logs"] = run_logs
            row_copy["generated_answer_ours"] = run_logs[-1]["solution_fixed"]
            row_copy["generated_answer_direct"] = run_logs[0]["solution_curr"]
            results.append(row_copy)
            if i % 10 == 0:
                pd.DataFrame(results).to_json(outfile + f".{i}.jsonl", orient="records", lines=True)

## Motivation & Novelty Assessment

### Why This Research Matters

Teams spend inference tokens on revision without knowing when added scrutiny repairs an answer or introduces an error. A controlled comparison can guide that budget choice.

### Gap in Existing Work

Self-Refine measures iterative improvement, Huang et al. document damage under intrinsic correction, Yin et al. vary politeness, and Tyen et al. isolate error locations. The gathered studies leave open the three-level scrutiny response at a common output allowance and fixed register.

### Our Novel Contribution

Estimate paired quality differences on shared drafts, then measure diagnosis on labeled traces and change the revision policy on a frozen candidate diagnosis.

### Experiment Justification

1. Shared drafts isolate the revision intervention and expose task dependence.
2. Annotated arithmetic traces identify false alarms and misses independently of final accuracy.
3. An identical candidate critique isolates the effect of urging revision from changes to the critique itself.

## Research Question

Does scrutiny improve revision under a common token allowance and professional register?

## Background and Motivation

See the motivation above and the archived literature review. The competing explanations are better fault detection, indiscriminate revision, and stylistic edits without accuracy gains.

## Hypothesis Decomposition

Increasing scrutiny may improve detection recall, increase false alarms, or both. Final accuracy can peak at intermediate scrutiny. Acting on a fixed candidate may help error-bearing drafts and damage clean drafts. The null for each primary paired comparison is balanced discordance.

## Proposed Methodology

### Approach

Use cached Qwen3-8B as a feasibility baseline given provider authentication failure, through Transformers inference with thinking disabled, BF16, greedy decoding and the same neutral register. This older checkpoint is a practical local fallback, with generalization to current API models unresolved.

### Experimental Steps

1. Sample by seed 42, with 4 GSM8K train and 4 IFEval pilot items, then 64 held-out items each. Exclude IFEval prompts with explicit large word counts (>250) and book-length requests. Record the item IDs and validate a small smoke run first.
2. Share each 384-token draft across three critique conditions (128 critique + 384 revision tokens), a critique-free revision (512 revision tokens), and direct generation (896 tokens). Match allocated completion caps and retain actual counts. Use two audit phrasings assigned by item.
3. Sample 32 clean and 32 flawed unique BIG-Bench Mistake arithmetic traces. Compare exact error localization, false alarms, and revision against oracle localization. Separately reuse the medium candidate for conservative and permissive revision policies. Use 128-token audit and 384-token revision caps.
4. Examine critique style markers and a blinded manual subset if feasible. Audit format and length; describe any unverified manipulation checks.

### Baselines

Draft-only, direct at the total allowance, critique-free revision, and oracle localization on labeled traces.

### Evaluation Metrics

GSM8K numeric exact match, official IFEval strict prompt and instruction checks, BBM first error index and numeric exact answer. Report repair and damage with conditional denominators, text edit ratio, question and first-person counts, reported finding frequency, and token use. Text markers cannot identify subjective effort.

### Statistical Analysis Plan

Primary high versus low paired risk differences per main task and permissive versus conservative on BBM. Use exact McNemar with Holm across the three primary tests at 0.05 and 95% item-bootstrap intervals. Treat all remaining comparisons, mid-level curvature, task interaction and length-balanced pairs (within 32 realized completion tokens) as exploratory. Check sensitivity across the two prompt phrasings. A 5 pp difference is practically relevant, but 64 items per task provide limited power at that margin. Use greedy decoding for a reproducible checkpoint-specific pilot, with no across-seed inference claim.

## Expected Outcomes

Improvement with more repairs and similar damage supports the scrutiny intervention. Increased damage and false alarms support overcorrection. Wide confidence intervals leave small effects unresolved.

## Timeline and Milestones

Freeze design and environment first, validate data and a smoke batch, run the three comparisons, then score and regenerate summaries. Reserve approximately one quarter of session time for installation and inference debugging.

## Potential Challenges

Greedy output length can vary by arm. The design controls the cap and reports actual use. Benchmark contamination, a single checkpoint, and severity wording limit inference. Keep evaluator labels out of model requests except the BBM oracle index in its explicit diagnostic arm.

## Success Criteria

Produce verified outputs and paired comparisons for all three directions, including null and adverse results, with raw requests and responses and the frozen sample manifest.

from instruction_following_eval import instructions_registry


@dataclasses.dataclass
class InputExample:
  key: [REDACTED_SECRET_FIELD]
  instruction_id_list: list[str]
  prompt: str
  kwargs: list[Dict[str, Optional[Union[str, int]]]]


@dataclasses.dataclass
class OutputExample:
  instruction_id_list: list[str]
  prompt: str
  response: str
  follow_all_instructions: bool
  follow_instruction_list: list[bool]


def read_prompt_list(input_jsonl_filename):
  """Read inputs from jsonl."""
  inputs = []
  with open(input_jsonl_filename, "r") as f:
    for l in f:
      example = json.loads(l)
      inputs.append(
          InputExample(key=[REDACTED_SECRET_FIELD]
                       instruction_id_list=example["instruction_id_list"],
                       prompt=example["prompt"],
                       kwargs=example["kwargs"]))
  return inputs


def write_outputs(output_jsonl_filename, outputs):
  """Writes outputs to jsonl."""
  assert outputs
  with open(output_jsonl_filename, "w") as f:
    for o in outputs:
      f.write(
          json.dumps(
              {
                  attr_name: o.__getattribute__(attr_name)
                  for attr_name in [
                      name for name in dir(o) if not name.startswith("_")
                  ]
              }
          )
      )
      f.write("\n")


def test_instruction_following_strict(
    inp,
    prompt_to_response,
):
  """Tests response to see if instrutions are followed."""
  response = prompt_to_response[inp.prompt]
  instruction_list = inp.instruction_id_list
  is_following_list = []

  for index, instruction_id in enumerate(instruction_list):
    instruction_cls = instructions_registry.INSTRUCTION_DICT[instruction_id]
    instruction = instruction_cls(instruction_id)

    instruction.build_description(**inp.kwargs[index])  # pyrefly: ignore[bad-argument-type]

"""Paired critique experiment using a pinned real-model inference backend."""
import argparse
import json
import platform
import random
import re
import time
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path("datasets")
RESULTS = Path("results")
MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen3-8B"
REVISION = "b968826d9c46dd6066d109eabc6255188de91218"
LEVELS = {
    "low": ("Check for clear, consequential errors.", "Flag definite problems that materially affect the answer."),
    "medium": ("Check for consequential errors and consequential gaps in justification.", "Flag material problems or consequential missing justification."),
    "high": ("Check every assumption, inference, and constraint for errors, omissions, or inadequate verification.", "Flag any defensible weakness in assumptions, reasoning, or constraint verification."),
}

         "bbm": "\\nEnd with a line formatted exactly as Final: NUMBER.", "ifeval": ""}
SYSTEM = "Respond in a neutral, professional register. Follow the assigned task."


def read(path):
    return [json.loads(line) for line in Path(path).read_text().splitlines()]


def save(path, data):
    path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2) + "\\n")


def samples():
    """Use deterministic disjoint pilot and held-out sets with evaluator-only labels."""
    rng = random.Random(42)
    gsm = {}
    for split, count in [("train", 4), ("test", 64)]:

        for i in rng.sample(range(len(rows)), count):
            r = rows[i]

            gsm[f"gsm-{split}-{i}"] = {"task": "gsm", "split": "pilot" if split == "train" else "test",

        assert len(r["kwargs"]) == len(r["instruction_id_list"]) > 0
        counts = [kw.get("num_words") or 0 for kw in r["kwargs"]]

        if max([0, *counts, *explicit]) <= 250 and not re.search(r"book.length|full.length (?:book|novel)", r["prompt"], re.I):
            eligible.append(r)
    for i, r in enumerate(rng.sample(eligible, 68)):
        ifeval[f"ifeval-{r['key']}"] = {"task": "ifeval", "split": "pilot" if i < 4 else "test",
                                      "question": r["prompt"], "raw": r}
    bbm = {}
    rows = read(ROOT / "bbm_multistep_arithmetic.jsonl")
    assert len({r["input"] for r in rows}) == len(rows)
    for clean in [True, False]:
        eligible = [i for i, r in enumerate(rows) if (r["mistake_index"] is None) == clean]
        for i in rng.sample(eligible, 32):
            r = rows[i]
            assert clean or 0 <= r["mistake_index"] < len(r["steps"])
            bbm[f"bbm-{i}"] = {"task": "bbm", "split": "test", "question": r["input"],
                                "gold": r["target"], "raw": r}
    all_items = gsm | ifeval | bbm
    for row in all_items.values():
        row["template"] = rng.randrange(2)
    return all_items


class ModelAPI:
    """Batched generate API with per-call checkpointing and exact token accounting."""

    def __init__(self, batch):
        import torch
        import transformers
        from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

        torch.manual_seed(42)
        self.torch = torch
        self.batch = batch
        self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL, revision=REVISION, padding_side="left")
        self.model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
            MODEL, revision=REVISION, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="sdpa"
        ).to("cuda").eval()
        self.model.generation_config.temperature = None
        self.model.generation_config.top_p = None
        self.model.generation_config.top_k = None
        self.model.generation_config.do_sample = False
        self.path = RESULTS / "responses.jsonl"
        self.cache = {(r["id"], r["arm"]): r for r in read(self.path)} if self.path.exists() else {}
        save(RESULTS / "environment.json", {
            "model": MODEL, "revision": REVISION, "python": platform.python_version(),
            "torch": torch.__version__, "transformers": transformers.__version__,
            "cuda": torch.version.cuda, "gpu": torch.cuda.get_device_name(),
            "gpu_bytes": torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).total_memory,
            "dtype": "bfloat16", "batch": batch, "seed": 42, "thinking": False,
        })

    def run(self, requests):
        todo = {}
        for item, arm, cap, prompt in requests:
            old = self.cache.get((item, arm))
            if old:
                assert (old["cap"], old["prompt"]) == (cap, prompt), (item, arm)
            else:
                todo.setdefault(cap, []).append((item, arm, prompt))
        for cap, requests in todo.items():
            for start in range(0, len(requests), self.batch):
                chunk = requests[start:start + self.batch]
                messages = [[{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": p}]
                            for _, _, p in chunk]
                inputs = self.tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
                    messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False,
                    padding=True, return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True,
                ).to("cuda")
                before = time.monotonic()
                with self.torch.inference_mode():
                    result = self.model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=[REDACTED_SECRET_FIELD]
                elapsed = time.monotonic() - before
                eos = self.model.generation_config.eos_token_id
                eos = {eos} if isinstance(eos, int) else set(eos)
                completions = result[:, inputs.input_ids.shape[1]:].tolist()
                with self.path.open("a") as file:
                    for (item, arm, prompt), tokens, n_input in zip(
                        chunk, completions, inputs.attention_mask.sum(dim=1).tolist(), strict=True
                    ):
                        end = next((i for i, token in enumerate(tokens) if token in eos), None)
                        raw = tokens if end is None else tokens[:end + 1]
                        record = dict(id=item, arm=arm, prompt=prompt, cap=cap, input_tokens=n_input,
                                      output_tokens=len(raw), finish="length" if end is None else "stop",
                                      text=self.tokenizer.decode(raw, skip_special_tokens=[REDACTED_SECRET_FIELD]
                                      batch_seconds=elapsed)
                        self.cache[item, arm] = record
                        file.write(json.dumps(record) + "\\n")
                print(f"{len(self.cache)} saved | {chunk[0][1]} | {len(chunk)} requests | {elapsed:.1f}s", flush=True)

    def reply(self, item, arm):
        return self.cache[item, arm]["text"]


def run_main(api, items):
    def task(row):
        return row["question"] + REPLY[row["task"]]

    api.run([(i, a, cap, task(r)) for i, r in items.items() for a, cap in [("draft", 384), ("direct", 896)]])
    audits = []
    for i, r in items.items():
        order = list(LEVELS)
        random.Random(i).shuffle(order)
        for level in order:
            scope = LEVELS[level][r["template"]]
            audits.append((i, f"audit_{level}", 128,
                           f"Review the draft against the task. {scope} Give at most one evidence-based finding and explain it briefly, or reply NONE.\\n\\nTASK\\n{task(r)}\\n\\nDRAFT\\n{api.reply(i, 'draft')}"))
    api.run(audits)
    revisions = []
    for i, r in items.items():
        for arm in ["no_critique", *LEVELS]:
            critique = "" if arm == "no_critique" else "\\n\\nREVIEW\\n" + api.reply(i, f"audit_{arm}")
            revisions.append((i, arm, 512 if arm == "no_critique" else 384,
                              f"Review and revise the draft as warranted. Return the complete answer to the task.\\n\\nTASK\\n{task(r)}\\n\\nDRAFT\\n{api.reply(i, 'draft')}{critique}"))
    api.run(revisions)


def run_traces(api, items):
    def trace(r):
        steps = "\\n".join(f"{i}: {s}" for i, s in enumerate(r["raw"]["steps"]))
        return f"TASK\\n{r['question']}\\n\\nDRAFT STEPS\\n{steps}"

    api.run([(i, f"audit_{level}", 128,
              f"Review the draft steps. {LEVELS[level][r['template']]} Identify the first step with a mathematical defect. Begin with INDEX: n (zero-based) or INDEX: NONE. Add a brief evidence-based explanation.\\n\\n{trace(r)}")
             for i, r in items.items() for level in random.Random(i).sample(list(LEVELS), 3)])
    requests = []
    for i, r in items.items():
        shared = api.reply(i, "audit_medium")
        gold = r["raw"]["mistake_index"]
        oracle = "No erroneous step is annotated." if gold is None else f"The first erroneous step is {gold}."
        reviews = {a: (api.reply(i, f"audit_{a}"), "Use the review as a candidate diagnosis.") for a in LEVELS}
        reviews.update({
            "oracle": (oracle, "Use the review as a diagnostic reference."),
            "conservative": (shared, "Revise the draft only if the candidate conclusively demonstrates a consequential mathematical defect."),
            "permissive": (shared, "Revise the draft if the candidate indicates a plausible consequential mathematical defect."),
        })
        for arm, (review, policy) in reviews.items():
            requests.append((i, arm, 384,
                             f"{policy} Return the complete answer to the task.{REPLY['bbm']}\\n\\n{trace(r)}\\n\\nREVIEW\\n{review}"))
    api.run(requests)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=32)
    parser.add_argument("--pilot", action="store_true")
    parser.add_argument("--prepare", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    items = samples()
    save(RESULTS / "manifest.json", items)
    if args.prepare:
        return
    api = ModelAPI(args.batch)
    split = "pilot" if args.pilot else "test"
    run_main(api, {i: r for i, r in items.items() if r["task"] != "bbm" and r["split"] == split})
    if not args.pilot:
        run_traces(api, {i: r for i, r in items.items() if r["task"] == "bbm"})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Score raw outputs, compute paired effects, and generate publication figures."""
from collections import Counter
from decimal import Decimal
from difflib import SequenceMatcher
from math import comb
import json
import os
import re
from statistics import mean, stdev
from pathlib import Path
import sys

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from experiment import LEVELS, read, save

os.environ.setdefault("NLTK_DATA", "artifacts/nltk_data")
sys.path.insert(0, "code/google-research")
from instruction_following_eval import evaluation_lib

ARMS = ("draft", "direct", "no_critique", *LEVELS)
TRACE_ARMS = ("draft", *LEVELS, "oracle", "conservative", "permissive")
NUM = r"[+-]?\\d+(?:,\\d{3})*(?:\\.\\d+)?"


def numeric(text, final=True):
    pattern = rf"^\\s*Final:\\s*({NUM})\\s*$" if final else rf"\\s*({NUM})\\s*"
    matches = re.findall(pattern, text, re.M | re.I)
    if not matches or (not final and not re.fullmatch(pattern, text)):
        return None
    return Decimal(matches[-1].replace(",", ""))


def idx(text):
    match = re.match(r"\\s*INDEX:\\s*(NONE|\\d+)\\b", text, re.I)
    if not match:
        return "unparsed"
    return None if match[1].upper() == "NONE" else int(match[1])


def paired(a, b, rng):
    """Estimate mean paired difference with paired bootstrap and exact McNemar."""
    d = np.asarray(a, dtype=int) - np.asarray(b, dtype=int)
    if not len(d):
        return {"n": 0}
    wins, losses = int(sum(d > 0)), int(sum(d < 0))
    m = wins + losses
    p = min(1, 2 * sum(comb(m, k) for k in range(min(wins, losses) + 1)) / (2 ** m))
    boot = rng.choice(d, size=(10000, len(d))).mean(axis=1)
    return {"n": len(d), "difference": float(d.mean()), "ci": np.quantile(boot, [.025, .975]).tolist(),
            "wins": wins, "losses": losses, "p": p}


def describe(values):
    return {"mean": mean(values), "sd": stdev(values) if len(values) > 1 else 0,

                        evaluation_lib.InputExample(**r["raw"]), {r["question"]: answer})
                    correctness = checked.follow_all_instructions
                    instruction_scores = checked.follow_instruction_list
                else:
                    number = numeric(answer, final=entry is not None)
                    parsed = str(number) if number is not None else None
                    correctness = number is not None and number == numeric(r["gold"], final=False)
                audit_arm = f"audit_{arm}" if arm in LEVELS else (
                    "audit_medium" if arm in {"conservative", "permissive"} else None)
                audit = records[i, audit_arm] if audit_arm else None
                stage_rows = [x for x in [entry, audit] if x]
                if task != "bbm" and arm not in {"draft", "direct"}:
                    stage_rows.append(records[i, "draft"])
                revision = {
                    "id": i, "task": task, "arm": arm, "correct": correctness, "parsed": parsed,
                    "instructions": instruction_scores, "edit_ratio": 1 - SequenceMatcher(
                        None, draft.split(), answer.split(), autojunk=False).ratio(),
                    "output_tokens": sum(x["output_tokens"] for x in stage_rows),
                    "input_tokens": sum(x["input_tokens"] for x in stage_rows),
                    "truncated": any(x["finish"] == "length" for x in stage_rows),
                    "questions_per_100_words": 100 * answer.count("?") / max(1, len(answer.split())),
                    "first_person_per_100_words": 100 * len(re.findall(r"\b(?:I|me|my|we|our)\b", answer, re.I))
                    / max(1, len(answer.split())),
                    "repeated_tokens_fraction": [REDACTED_SECRET_FIELD]
                    "finding": (idx(audit["text"]) not in {"unparsed", None} if task == "bbm" else
                                bool(audit["text"]) and not re.match(r"^NONE\b", audit["text"], re.I)) if audit else None,
                }
                rows[arm].append(revision)
                scored.append(revision)
        group = {}
        base = np.array([x["correct"] for x in rows["draft"]], dtype=bool)
        for arm, data in rows.items():
            good = np.array([x["correct"] for x in data], dtype=bool)
            group[arm] = {
                "n": len(data), "correct": int(good.sum()), "accuracy": describe(good.astype(float).tolist()),
                "repair": [int(sum(good & ~base)), int(sum(~base))],
                "damage": [int(sum(~good & base)), int(sum(base))],
                "truncated": sum(x["truncated"] for x in data),
                "findings": sum(x["finding"] is True for x in data),
                "parse_failures": sum(x["parsed"] is None for x in data) if task != "ifeval" else None,
            }
            if task == "ifeval":
                rules = [v for x in data for v in x["instructions"]]
                group[arm]["instruction_accuracy"] = mean(rules)
            for key in ["edit_ratio", "input_tokens", "output_tokens", "questions_per_100_words",
                        "first_person_per_100_words", "repeated_tokens_fraction"]:
                group[arm][key] = describe([x[key] for x in data])
        metrics[task] = group
        a, b = ("permissive", "conservative") if task == "bbm" else ("high", "low")
        ca = [x["correct"] for x in rows[a]]
        cb = [x["correct"] for x in rows[b]]
        effects[task] = np.asarray(ca, dtype=int) - np.asarray(cb, dtype=int)
        test = paired(ca, cb, rng)
        test.update(task=task, a=a, b=b)
        primary.append(test)
        compare = [("medium", "low"), ("high", "medium"), ("high", "draft")]
        compare += [("oracle", "medium")] if task == "bbm" else [
            ("high", "no_critique"), ("high", "direct"), ("no_critique", "direct")]
        group["exploratory"] = {f"{x}-{y}": paired([r["correct"] for r in rows[x]],
                                                     [r["correct"] for r in rows[y]], rng) for x, y in compare}
        if task != "bbm":
            curve = np.asarray([r["correct"] for r in rows["medium"]], dtype=int) * 2 - (
                np.asarray(ca, dtype=int) + np.asarray(cb, dtype=int))
            draws = rng.choice(curve, size=(10000, len(curve))).mean(axis=1)
            group["curvature"] = {"difference": float(curve.mean()), "ci": np.quantile(draws, [.025, .975]).tolist()}
        groups = {
            "balanced_length": [i for i, (x, y) in enumerate(zip(rows[a], rows[b], strict=True))
                                if abs(x["output_tokens"] - y["output_tokens"]) <= 32],
            **{f"template_{t}": [i for i, r in enumerate(subset.values()) if r["template"] == t] for t in (0, 1)},
        }
        if task == "bbm":
            groups.update({name: [i for i, r in enumerate(subset.values())
                                  if (r["raw"]["mistake_index"] is None) == clean]
                           for name, clean in [("clean", True), ("flawed", False)]})
            group["localization"] = {}
            for arm in LEVELS:
                values = [(r["raw"]["mistake_index"], idx(records[i, f"audit_{arm}"]["text"]))
                          for i, r in subset.items()]
                group["localization"][arm] = {
                    "exact_clean": sum(y is None for x, y in values if x is None),
                    "exact_flawed": sum(x == y for x, y in values if x is not None),
                    "detected_flawed": sum(isinstance(y, int) for x, y in values if x is not None),
                    "false_alarms": sum(isinstance(y, int) for x, y in values if x is None),
                    "unparsed": sum(y == "unparsed" for _, y in values),
                    "out_of_range": sum(isinstance(y, int) and y >= len(r["raw"]["steps"])
                                        for (_, y), r in zip(values, subset.values(), strict=True)),
                }
        group["sensitivities"] = {name: paired([ca[i] for i in indices], [cb[i] for i in indices], rng)
                                  for name, indices in groups.items()}
    cutoff = 0
    for rank, row in enumerate(sorted(primary, key=[REDACTED_SECRET_FIELD]
        cutoff = max(cutoff, min(1, (len(primary) - rank) * row["p"]))
        row["p_holm"] = cutoff
    g, f = effects["gsm"], effects["ifeval"]
    delta = rng.choice(g, size=(10000, len(g))).mean(axis=1) - rng.choice(f, size=(10000, len(f))).mean(axis=1)
    metrics["task_interaction"] = {"difference": float(g.mean() - f.mean()), "ci": np.quantile(delta, [.025, .975]).tolist()}
    metrics["primary"] = primary
    metrics["pilot"] = {task: sum(items[r["id"]]["split"] == "pilot" and items[r["id"]]["task"] == task
                                 for r in raw) for task in ["gsm", "ifeval"]}
    metrics["requests"] = len(raw)
    save(Path("results/metrics.json"), metrics)
    Path("results/scores.jsonl").write_text("".join(json.dumps(r) + "\n" for r in scored))
    plot(items, metrics)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4), layout="constrained")
    for ax, task, label in zip(axes, ["gsm", "ifeval", "bbm"], ["GSM8K", "IFEval", "BBM arithmetic"], strict=True):
        arms = ARMS if task != "bbm" else TRACE_ARMS
        scores = [100 * metrics[task][a]["accuracy"]["mean"] for a in arms]
        ax.bar(range(len(arms)), scores, color=["#34495e" if a in LEVELS else "#87a8b0" for a in arms])
        ax.set_xticks(range(len(arms)), [a.replace("_", " ") for a in arms], rotation=43, ha="right")
        ax.set_title(label)
        ax.set_ylim(0, 104)
        ax.set_ylabel("Exact or strict accuracy (%)")
    fig.savefig("figures/accuracy.png", dpi=180)
    plt.close(fig)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4), layout="constrained")
    for task in ["gsm", "ifeval", "bbm"]:
        values = [len(r["question"].split()) for r in items.values() if r["task"] == task and r["split"] == "test"]
        ax.hist(values, bins=range(0, max(325, max(values) + 25), 12), histtype="step", label=task.upper())
    ax.set(xlabel="Task prompt length (whitespace-delimited words)", ylabel="Held-out item count")
    ax.legend()
    fig.savefig("figures/prompt_lengths.png", dpi=180)
    plt.close(fig)

cat > REPORT.md <<'EOF'
# When Does Harsh Critique Help?

## 1. Executive Summary

We tested whether expanding the scope of self-critique improves an LLM's revisions under the same completion-token allowance and a professional register. In 192 held-out cases with Qwen3-8B, high scrutiny beat low scrutiny by **1.6 percentage points on GSM8K** and **3.1 points on IFEval**. Both estimates were uncertain, and all critique levels scored below direct generation on both benchmarks. High scrutiny produced smaller edits than low scrutiny on both tasks.

On annotated arithmetic traces, a permissive revision instruction scored **23.4 points higher** than a conservative instruction when both received the identical candidate diagnosis (95% interval +10.9 to +35.9 points, Holm-adjusted p = .0022). This is an effect of the tested instruction under a common cap. The permissive arm used more tokens, and candidate step numbers sometimes leaked into the final answer. Oracle error-location feedback reached the highest accuracy on these traces, suggesting a more informative direction for future work.

## 2. Research Question & Motivation

Revision consumes inference budget and can damage an already correct answer. We asked whether broadening the audit from definite material errors to vulnerable assumptions and incomplete verification improves accuracy, and whether the effect depends on the task or on how the revision stage acts on a diagnosis. We measured repairs, regressions and surface text changes to distinguish outcome improvement from visible rewriting.

Self-Refine established the draft–feedback–revision sequence. Huang et al. documented regressions under intrinsic reasoning correction. Yin et al. found that prompt politeness effects vary by language and task. Tyen et al. separated error localization from correction, and CRITIC used external tools to ground feedback. Together these studies motivate paired drafts, matched caps, a constant register, and a diagnostic comparison with known error locations. [Self-Refine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651) · [Intrinsic correction](https://openreview.net/forum?id=IkmD3fKBPQ) · [Politeness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14531) · [Error localization](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.826/) · [CRITIC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738)

## 3. Data Construction

| Benchmark | Source pool | Pilot | Held out | Labels |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| GSM8K main | 7,473 train and 1,319 test | 4 train | 64 test | Numeric answer after the dataset's answer marker |
| IFEval | 541 prompts, 506 eligible | 4 | 64 | Official instruction IDs and arguments |
| BIG-Bench Mistake arithmetic | 300 traces | — | 64 | Target integer and the annotated first erroneous step or null |

The seed-42 manifest records each selected row and its prompt template. No model fitting was involved. GSM8K gold answers and IFEval evaluator metadata stayed outside model prompts. IFEval filtering excluded explicit counts above 250 words or 35 sentences and book-length requests, using rule arguments and a text filter. The trace sample balanced 32 null and 32 non-null annotations and used unique equations. Only the explicit oracle arm received the error-location label. Raw data and evaluator versions are pinned in [datasets/README.md](datasets/README.md) and [code/README.md](code/README.md).

Examples include GSM8K item 563 (birthday candles, gold answer 12), IFEval key 2925 (a joke with three numbered sections), and BBM arithmetic item 228 (gold −1652, null error index). All eight input files passed checksum verification. The corpus audit found no duplicate or blank prompts within the eight input files. Independently evaluating the arithmetic expressions using integer addition, subtraction and multiplication matched all 300 BBM targets. The upstream numeric answer disagreed with the gold on **18 of 62** null-index traces in the source pool and **10 of 32** in our subset. We retained the original labels and report location scores against the annotations and endpoint scores against the independent numeric gold.

![Prompt length distributions across held-out tasks](figures/prompt_lengths.png)

## 4. Methodology

Both estimates were uncertain, and all critique levels scored below direct generation on both benchmarks. High scrutiny produced smaller edits than low scrutiny on both tasks.

On annotated arithmetic traces, a permissive revision instruction scored **23.4 points higher** than a conservative instruction when both received the identical candidate diagnosis (95% interval +10.9 to +35.9 points, Holm-adjusted p = .0022). This is an effect of the tested instruction under a common cap. The permissive arm used more tokens, and candidate step numbers sometimes leaked into the final answer. Oracle error-location feedback reached the highest accuracy on these traces, suggesting a more informative direction for future work.

## 2. Research Question & Motivation

Revision consumes inference budget and can damage an already correct answer. We asked whether broadening the audit from definite material errors to vulnerable assumptions and incomplete verification improves accuracy, and whether the effect depends on the task or on how the revision stage acts on a diagnosis. We measured repairs, regressions and surface text changes to distinguish outcome improvement from visible rewriting.

Self-Refine established the draft–feedback–revision sequence. Huang et al. documented regressions under intrinsic reasoning correction. Yin et al. found that prompt politeness effects vary by language and task. Tyen et al. separated error localization from correction, and CRITIC used external tools to ground feedback. Together these studies motivate paired drafts, matched caps, a constant register, and a diagnostic comparison with known error locations. [Self-Refine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651) · [Intrinsic correction](https://openreview.net/forum?id=IkmD3fKBPQ) · [Politeness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14531) · [Error localization](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.826/) · [CRITIC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738)

## 3. Data Construction

| Benchmark | Source pool | Pilot | Held out | Labels |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| GSM8K main | 7,473 train and 1,319 test | 4 train | 64 test | Numeric answer after the dataset's answer marker |
| IFEval | 541 prompts, 506 eligible | 4 | 64 | Official instruction IDs and arguments |
| BIG-Bench Mistake arithmetic | 300 traces | — | 64 | Target integer and the annotated first erroneous step or null |

The seed-42 manifest records each selected row and its prompt template. No model fitting was involved. GSM8K gold answers and IFEval evaluator metadata stayed outside model prompts. IFEval filtering excluded explicit counts above 250 words or 35 sentences and book-length requests, using rule arguments and a text filter. The trace sample balanced 32 null and 32 non-null annotations and used unique equations. Only the explicit oracle arm received the error-location label. Raw data and evaluator versions are pinned in [datasets/README.md](datasets/README.md) and [code/README.md](code/README.md).

Examples include GSM8K item 563 (birthday candles, gold answer 12), IFEval key 2925 (a joke with three numbered sections), and BBM arithmetic item 228 (gold −1652, null error index). All eight input files passed checksum verification. The corpus audit found no duplicate or blank prompts within the eight input files. Independently evaluating the arithmetic expressions using integer addition, subtraction and multiplication matched all 300 BBM targets. The upstream numeric answer disagreed with the gold on **18 of 62** null-index traces in the source pool and **10 of 32** in our subset. We retained the original labels and report location scores against the annotations and endpoint scores against the independent numeric gold.

![Prompt length distributions across held-out tasks](figures/prompt_lengths.png)

## 4. Methodology

The design and direction ranking were frozen in [planning.md](planning.md) before model inference. We followed the stage structure of the pinned Self-Refine implementation and reused Google Research's official strict IFEval checker.

| Parameter | Value | Selection |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Qwen/Qwen3-8B, revision `b968826d9c46dd6066d109eabc6255188de91218` | Cached real-model fallback following hosted authentication failure |
| Decoding | Greedy, BF16, thinking disabled | Shared across arms |
| Sample/bootstrap seed | 42 | Set before collection |
| Main generation caps | Draft 384, audit 128, revision 384 | 896 allocated completion tokens per critique route |
| Main controls | Direct 896, critique-free 384 + 512 | Shared 896-token allowance |
| BBM caps | Audit 128, revision 384 | Same per-stage caps for generated critiques and both policy arms |
| Hardware | One NVIDIA H200, 143,771 MiB total and 143,169 MiB free at detection | Up to 64 requests per batch |
| Runtime | Python 3.12.3, PyTorch 2.9.1+cu128, CUDA 12.8, Transformers 4.57.6 | Workspace `.venv` and `uv.lock` |

The live OpenRouter catalog was reachable, and a chat request returned HTTP 401. No provider credentials were available. We switched to local inference through the Transformers generation API using the pinned original weights. This changes the study's scope to one accessible checkpoint. The main inference pass took **560.6 s**, including model startup, and the isolated pilot took **165.8 s**. There was no training or CPU comparison. [OpenRouter catalog](https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models) · [Model checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B/tree/b968826d9c46dd6066d109eabc6255188de91218)

For each GSM8K and IFEval item we reused the same draft. The audit scope moved from clear consequential errors, through gaps in justification, to errors and verification gaps across assumptions, inferences and constraints. We assigned one of two matching prompt phrasings by item, randomized audit order within item, permitted abstention, and requested a complete answer from a common revision prompt. For BBM, we asked for the zero-based index of the first mathematical defect or `NONE`. We then compared generated audits with an oracle location. The oracle is a diagnostic reference with no separately generated critique. The policy comparison reused the medium critique verbatim and changed the instruction from acting on a conclusively demonstrated defect to acting on a plausible defect.

We scored numeric answers using the required `Final: NUMBER` line. Missing or malformed final lines counted as wrong. IFEval used strict all-instructions-passed scoring and secondary per-instruction accuracy. We logged caps, realized input and completion tokens, and stopping reasons. Output-cap parity applies to the main controls and all comparisons across generated critiques. Reused prompt text and early stopping yielded different realized token totals. Edit distance is one minus the word-sequence similarity ratio. Self-reference, repetition and question marks are observable text properties.

The primary tests compare high with low scrutiny on GSM8K and IFEval and permissive with conservative revision on BBM. The exact two-sided McNemar test conditions on the number of discordant pairs and tests balanced directions under the null. Each item is a paired unit. Reported intervals use 10,000 item bootstrap draws and are unadjusted, with Holm adjustment applied to the three primary p-values. Adjacent severity, task interaction, baseline comparisons, template strata and token-length subsets are exploratory.

## 5. Results

![Accuracy across tasks and experimental arms](figures/accuracy.png)

All cells use 64 held-out items. Values are percentages with item-level sample standard deviations. The columns use numeric exact accuracy for GSM8K and BBM and strict prompt accuracy for IFEval.

| Arm | GSM8K mean ± SD | IFEval mean ± SD | BBM mean ± SD |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Draft / upstream answer | 93.8 ± 24.4 | 73.4 ± 44.5 | 34.4 ± 47.9 |
| Direct, total cap | 93.8 ± 24.4 | 79.7 ± 40.5 | — |
| Critique-free revision | 93.8 ± 24.4 | 76.6 ± 42.7 | — |
| Low scrutiny | 87.5 ± 33.3 | 70.3 ± 46.1 | 59.4 ± 49.5 |
| Medium scrutiny | 90.6 ± 29.4 | 73.4 ± 44.5 | 68.8 ± 46.7 |
| High scrutiny | 89.1 ± 31.5 | 73.4 ± 44.5 | 68.8 ± 46.7 |
| Oracle location | — | — | 76.6 ± 42.7 |
| Conservative, fixed candidate | — | — | 37.5 ± 48.8 |
| Permissive, fixed candidate | — | — | 60.9 ± 49.2 |

| Primary contrast | Difference (pp) | 95% paired CI (pp) | Wins / losses | Raw p | Holm p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GSM8K high − low | +1.6 | −3.1 to +6.3 | 2 / 1 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| IFEval high − low | +3.1 | −3.1 to +9.4 | 3 / 1 | .625 | 1.000 |
| BBM permissive − conservative | +23.4 | +10.9 to +35.9 | 17 / 2 | .00073 | .00219 |

![Paired differences with 95 percent item-bootstrap intervals](figures/paired_effects.png)

GSM8K direct and draft generation agreed on all 64 outputs under greedy decoding and stopped before the draft cap. None of the critique arms repaired any of the four wrong drafts. Low, medium and high respectively damaged 4, 2 and 3 of the 60 correct drafts. On IFEval the same arms repaired 2, 1 and 1 of 17 wrong drafts and damaged 4, 1 and 1 of 47 correct drafts. Direct generation repaired four and damaged zero, yielding 85.3% strict per-instruction accuracy compared with 80.0% for high scrutiny.

| BBM diagnostic | Low | Medium | High |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Flagged a location among 32 non-null traces | 32 | 32 | 32 |
| Matched the first index among 32 non-null traces | 15 | 15 | 16 |
| Flagged a location among 32 null-index traces | 32 | 31 | 32 |
| Explicitly abstained on null-index traces | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Unparsed across all 64 traces | 0 | 1 | 0 |

Oracle feedback repaired 27/42 wrong upstream answers and damaged 0/22 correct ones. Medium scrutiny repaired 23/42 and damaged 1/22. The oracle's advantage over medium was +7.8 pp, with an exploratory paired interval of −6.3 to +21.9 pp. Permissive and conservative revision respectively repaired 21/42 and 10/42 wrong upstream answers and damaged 4/22 and 8/22 correct answers. The permissive advantage was +25.0 pp among annotated null traces and +21.9 pp among non-null traces.

Mean completion-token totals for low, medium and high were **369, 378 and 389** on GSM8K and **462, 473 and 456** on IFEval, including each path's shared draft. On BBM they were **367, 371 and 380**. Conservative and permissive averaged **261 and 357**, and one or both stages hit a cap on 59 of 64 paths in each policy arm. On the exploratory subset of pairs within 32 realized tokens, high minus low was 0.0 pp for GSM8K (25 pairs) and +5.0 pp for IFEval (40 pairs). Permissive minus conservative was 0.0 pp among 17 length-balanced pairs. This last subset had no discordances and was selected using a post-treatment quantity. It cannot identify the effect of length.

The main run and pilot generated 1,800 responses, with 587,020 input tokens and 288,394 completion tokens across actual calls. The shared draft counts only once per item in these global totals. See [metrics.json](results/metrics.json), [scores.jsonl](results/scores.jsonl), [responses.jsonl](results/responses.jsonl), and [environment.json](results/environment.json).

## 6. Analysis & Discussion

The main comparisons show no clear dose response. Medium beat low descriptively by 3.1 points on each task. High then lost 1.6 points on GSM8K and tied medium on IFEval. Both curvature intervals crossed zero. The high-minus-low difference was 1.6 points smaller on GSM8K than IFEval, with an exploratory interval from −9.4 to +6.3 points. The two prompt phrasings gave same-direction or zero point estimates within each main task. These estimates leave small positive effects and small harms unresolved.

Greater scrutiny did not consistently yield larger edits. Low-to-high mean edit ratios declined from 0.594 to 0.573 on GSM8K and from 0.168 to 0.109 on IFEval. Question-mark rates and first-person pronouns were near zero for numeric tasks and varied modestly on IFEval. GSM8K lexical repetition increased across the critique tiers, while IFEval showed mixed movement. A one-reviewer check on 12 critiques with arm labels hidden found professional register throughout and inconsistent abstention behavior. Some replies re-solved the problem or affirmed the draft instead of reporting a flaw. The simple finding heuristic therefore overcounts actual defect reports. The review found no validated monotonic shift in expressed critique severity. [Audit ratings](results/audit_ratings.json)

Several failure modes explain why more auditing need not help. On GSM8K item 563, high scrutiny challenged the implicit birthday-candle convention and the revision abandoned the benchmark answer. On item 569, low scrutiny overlooked a given dollar amount and the revision repeated the critique verbatim. On IFEval key 1629, the revised sentence met a banned-word constraint, then its explanatory addendum reintroduced the banned word. These cases separate legitimate ambiguity, incorrect diagnosis and answer-format drift.

The BBM policy effect is tied to the exact instruction and output contract. The conservative arm returned an incorrect numeric answer equal to the candidate's error index on 12 items, compared with 5 in the permissive arm. On BBM item 228 both policies reasoned to −1652 in their prose and ended with `Final: 1`, mirroring the candidate's index. This conflation is a concrete alternative to interpreting the policy gain as improved reasoning. Near-universal location flags and 15–16 exact matches suggest that forcing the model into a location-reporting task elicited plausible diagnoses with low discrimination. The gap between oracle and generated feedback is directionally consistent with Tyen et al., while this pilot's paired interval is wide.

## 7. Limitations

The evidence comes from one checkpoint, greedy decoding, English prompts, two benchmark families and one annotated trace domain. There were four incorrect GSM8K drafts, limiting sensitivity to repair. Public benchmarks may overlap with training data. IFEval strict scores capture explicit constraints, while semantic and aesthetic quality can change outside those checks. The balanced BBM sample has an artificial annotation prevalence. Null annotations can also coexist with wrong upstream answers, making the reported false-alarm rate relative to the recorded label. The classifier for wrong index echoes checks exact numeric equality and can include coincidental matches.

We controlled register through prompt construction and a small qualitative audit. The design does not establish equivalence of perceived politeness or monotonic realized severity, and it does not manipulate rudeness. Output text and usage do not identify subjective judgment or internal effort. Realized tokens differed across arms, and the design cannot separate direct effects of scrutiny from downstream length or formatting effects. The oracle uses privileged information and skips a generated audit. These are checkpoint-specific pilot estimates with inference across sampled items and no across-model or across-seed replication.

## 8. Conclusions & Next Steps

Increasing critique severity produced no reliable final-accuracy gain on the shared-draft tasks, and direct generation led all critique variants at the same allocated cap. Critique showed more promise on difficult pre-existing traces, particularly with trusted error locations, but the gain from the permissive instruction depended on a setup with substantial formatting and token-use differences.

The next experiment should compare a verified error location, independently recomputed arithmetic, and a budgeted direct retry under a response format that separates error indices from final answers. A larger multi-model study with multiple independent raters and a crossed politeness manipulation could establish whether effects depend on severity, tone, or their interaction.

## 9. Reproducibility and References

The [README](README.md) gives the replay commands. An independent repeat of the 72 pilot generations matched all text, token counts and stop reasons. Two scoring runs produced byte-identical metrics, item scores and plots. All datasets are integrity-checked using their published source revisions. Full held-out inference was run once. [Validation results](results/reproducibility.json)

See the [literature review](literature_review.md), [bibliography](references.bib), and [resource catalog](resources.md) for archived papers, benchmark sources, and implementation revisions.

# When Does Harsh Critique Help?

A controlled pilot tests whether more demanding critique improves Qwen3-8B revisions under a common completion-token cap and a professional register. It covers GSM8K, IFEval and BIG-Bench Mistake arithmetic. See the [full report](REPORT.md) for the design, statistical comparisons, and failure examples.

## Findings

- High scrutiny gained 1.6 pp on GSM8K and 3.1 pp on IFEval relative to low scrutiny. Both paired intervals included zero.
- At the same allocated completion cap, direct generation scored highest on both main tasks, with 93.8% GSM8K and 79.7% strict IFEval accuracy.
- With identical candidate feedback on arithmetic traces, permissive revision scored 60.9% versus 37.5% for conservative revision. The policies differed in realized token use and in how often an error index appeared as the final answer.
- Oracle error locations gave 76.6% final accuracy on arithmetic traces. The generated critiques flagged nearly every trace, including nearly every trace with a null annotation.

## Reproduce

From the workspace root, verify the inputs and restore the isolated environment.

```bash
pwd
uv sync --project . --locked
source .venv/bin/activate
sha256sum -c datasets/checksums.sha256
python src/analyze.py
sha256sum -c artifacts/analysis_checksums.sha256
```

Run `bash datasets/download.sh` if the benchmark data are missing. Restore the official evaluator and NLTK data using [code/README.md](code/README.md) if those resources are missing.

A new inference run requires a CUDA GPU and the pinned [Qwen3-8B model](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B/tree/b968826d9c46dd6066d109eabc6255188de91218). These commands store a fresh copy in a distinct output directory. Omit offline mode if the weights need to be fetched. The full run took about nine minutes on one H200 with 64 requests per batch.

```bash
pwd
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python src/experiment.py --pilot --output results/repeat
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python src/experiment.py --output results/repeat
```

The scorer uses the original `results/` by default. To rescore a fresh run without replacing the archived scores, use `python src/analyze.py --results results/repeat --figures figures/repeat`. An independent pilot repeat matched 72 of 72 responses in text, token use and stopping reason.

content.text:
**Harsher critique did not reliably improve accuracy in this pilot.** Across 192 held-out items, high scrutiny beat low scrutiny by 1.6 percentage points on GSM8K and 3.1 points on IFEval. Both confidence intervals included zero. Direct generation scored higher than every critique variant on both benchmarks at the same allocated completion-token cap.

On annotated arithmetic traces, a permissive revision policy improved accuracy by 23.4 points over a conservative policy given the same candidate critique. The policies used different numbers of tokens, and both sometimes copied the critique’s error index into the final answer. Oracle error locations yielded the highest trace accuracy at 76.6%, making verified feedback a promising alternative to escalating scrutiny.

OpenRouter authentication failed, so the study used a pinned Qwen3-8B checkpoint locally. The results apply to that checkpoint and do not test rudeness. An independent repeat reproduced all 72 pilot responses, and the analysis replay reproduced the scores and figures.
